# Appendix: RF Circuit Simulation {#sec-simulation}

There is no breadboard for an integrated circuit: every design decision in an RFIC is checked by circuit simulation before tapeout. A SPICE-type simulator [@Nagel.1975] offers a small set of **fundamental analyses** (dc operating point, small-signal ac and noise, and transient), which are perfectly adequate for amplifiers, filters, and bias circuits. RF circuits, however, push these analyses to their limits, for several reasons:

::: {.content-hidden when-format="revealjs"}
- **Widely separated time scales.** An LO at several GHz carries information at kHz to MHz offsets, and flicker noise matters down to a few Hz. A time-domain simulation must resolve the fastest signal for as long as the slowest one needs.
- **Large periodic signals.** The LO of a mixer, the clock of a switched-capacitor filter, or the carrier of a PA moves the operating point periodically. With respect to the small signal, such a circuit is *time-variant* (see @sec-mixer-time-variant), so an analysis linearized around a constant operating point cannot capture its behavior.
- **Frequency translation of noise.** In such time-variant circuits, noise is modulated by the large signal and folded from many frequencies onto the wanted output frequency.
- **High-Q resonators and oscillators.** High-Q circuits take many periods to settle, and an oscillator has no stable dc operating point at all. Its frequency and phase noise are results of the large-signal operation.
:::

::: {.content-visible when-format="revealjs"}
- **Widely separated time scales**: GHz LO, kHz to MHz signal, Hz flicker noise
- **Large periodic signals** (LO, clock, carrier): the circuit is *time-variant* for the small signal (@sec-mixer-time-variant)
- **Frequency translation of noise**: modulated and folded noise
- **High-Q resonators and oscillators**: long settling, no stable dc operating point
:::

These challenges led to a set of **advanced RF analyses**: transient noise, periodic steady-state analysis by shooting (PSS) and by harmonic balance (HB), and the small-signal (PAC, HBAC) and noise (PNOISE, HBNOISE) analyses built on top of a periodic steady state [@Kundert.1999]. For a long time, the complete set was only available in commercial simulators, while open-source simulators offered parts of it (e.g., harmonic balance in Xyce, and transient-noise sources and an experimental oscillator PSS in ngspice). Since September 2026, the development version of the open-source simulator VACASK [@Buermen.2025] supports all of them. They are not part of a tagged VACASK release yet, but the [IIC-OSIC-TOOLS](https://github.com/iic-jku/IIC-OSIC-TOOLS) container ships them from its release 2026.10 on, so that the complete RF verification flow of this appendix can be run with open-source tools. The analysis names used in this appendix follow VACASK, which largely uses the names of Cadence Spectre (Spectre calls the operating point `dc` and the S-parameter analysis `sp`). @sec-simulation-tools lists the corresponding ngspice commands.

@fig-sim-analysis-overview shows how the analyses build on each other. All of them start from the dc operating point. The small-signal analyses linearize the circuit either around this constant operating point, which gives a linear time-invariant (LTI) system, or around a periodic steady state, which gives a linear periodically time-varying (LPTV) system.

{{< include /content/simulation/_fig_sim_analysis_overview.qmd >}}

All analyses solve the same circuit equations. With modified nodal analysis (MNA), a circuit is described by

$$
\mathbf{f}(\mathbf{x}(t)) + \frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t} \mathbf{q}(\mathbf{x}(t)) = \mathbf{u}(t),
$$ {#eq-sim-circuit-equations}

where the vector $\mathbf{x}$ contains the unknown node voltages and selected branch currents (of inductors and voltage sources), $\mathbf{f}$ the currents of the resistive elements (summed per node according to Kirchhoff's current law) together with the branch equations of voltage sources and inductors, $\mathbf{q}$ the charges of capacitors and fluxes of inductors, and $\mathbf{u}$ the independent sources. The analyses differ only in the assumption they make about $\mathbf{x}(t)$:

::: {.content-hidden when-format="revealjs"}
- **dc operating point**: all time derivatives vanish, $\mathbf{f}(\mathbf{x}_0) = \mathbf{u}_\mathrm{DC}$.
- **ac and noise**: a small deviation from $\mathbf{x}_0$, so that @eq-sim-circuit-equations can be linearized around $\mathbf{x}_0$ (LTI).
- **transient**: no assumption at all. The time derivative is discretized, and @eq-sim-circuit-equations is integrated step by step.
- **PSS and HB**: the solution is periodic, $\mathbf{x}(t + T) = \mathbf{x}(t)$ (or quasi-periodic for several incommensurate tones in HB).
- **PAC, PNOISE, HBAC, HBNOISE**: a small deviation from a periodic steady state $\mathbf{x}_\mathrm{s}(t)$, so that @eq-sim-circuit-equations can be linearized around $\mathbf{x}_\mathrm{s}(t)$ (LPTV).
:::

::: {.content-visible when-format="revealjs"}
- **op**: $\mathrm{d}/\mathrm{d}t = 0$, $\mathbf{f}(\mathbf{x}_0) = \mathbf{u}_\mathrm{DC}$
- **ac, noise**: linearized around $\mathbf{x}_0$ (LTI)
- **tran**: no assumption, integrate in time
- **PSS, HB**: $\mathbf{x}(t + T) = \mathbf{x}(t)$
- **PAC, PNOISE, HBAC, HBNOISE**: linearized around $\mathbf{x}_\mathrm{s}(t)$ (LPTV)
:::

## Fundamental Analyses {#sec-simulation-fundamental}

### DC Operating Point and DC Sweep {#sec-simulation-op}

The **operating point** analysis (`op`) sets all time derivatives in @eq-sim-circuit-equations to zero (capacitors become open circuits, inductors short circuits) and solves the remaining nonlinear algebraic equations $\mathbf{f}(\mathbf{x}_0) = \mathbf{u}_\mathrm{DC}$ with the Newton-Raphson method. Starting from an initial guess $\mathbf{x}^{(0)}$, it iterates

$$
\mathbf{G}(\mathbf{x}^{(i)}) \, \Delta \mathbf{x}^{(i)} = \mathbf{u}_\mathrm{DC} - \mathbf{f}(\mathbf{x}^{(i)}), \qquad \mathbf{x}^{(i+1)} = \mathbf{x}^{(i)} + \Delta \mathbf{x}^{(i)},
$$ {#eq-sim-newton}

where $\mathbf{G} = \partial \mathbf{f} / \partial \mathbf{x}$ is the Jacobian (the conductance matrix of the linearized circuit). Each iteration requires the solution of a sparse linear system. Newton-Raphson converges very fast close to the solution but can fail from a poor starting point. Simulators therefore fall back to continuation methods such as gmin stepping (temporarily adding conductances to ground) or source stepping (ramping up the supplies). The same Newton iteration is the inner engine of every other analysis in this appendix.

A **dc sweep** (`.dc` in ngspice, a `sweep` around `op` in VACASK) repeats the operating point analysis while stepping a source or a parameter, using each solution as the starting point of the next one. It yields static transfer characteristics, e.g., the dc output of a power detector versus a bias voltage, or the multiplier characteristic of a Gilbert cell (@sec-mixer-gilbert).

::: {.callout-important}
## Always Check the Operating Point First
Every small-signal analysis (ac, acsp, noise) linearizes around the operating point and inherits all its errors. Check bias currents, $\gmid$ values, and saturation margins before looking at any other result. Note also that circuits with positive feedback (latches, oscillators) have an operating point that is an *unstable* equilibrium: it is a valid solution of the equations, but the real circuit never stays there. For bistable circuits, the operating point may not converge at all, and a defined state (a reset or a nodeset) helps.
:::

### Small-Signal AC Analysis {#sec-simulation-ac}

The **ac analysis** (`ac`) assumes a small sinusoidal excitation, $\mathbf{x}(t) = \mathbf{x}_0 + \mathrm{Re}\{\mathbf{X} e^{j \omega t}\}$, and linearizes @eq-sim-circuit-equations around the operating point. In the frequency domain, this gives one complex linear system per frequency:

$$
\left( \mathbf{G} + j \omega \mathbf{C} \right) \mathbf{X}(j\omega) = \mathbf{U}(j\omega), \qquad \mathbf{G} = \frac{\partial \mathbf{f}}{\partial \mathbf{x}}, \quad \mathbf{C} = \frac{\partial \mathbf{q}}{\partial \mathbf{x}},
$$ {#eq-sim-ac}

with both Jacobians evaluated at $\mathbf{x}_0$. As the system is linear, the amplitude of the source is arbitrary (usually 1 V), and the results are transfer functions: gain, phase, bandwidth, input and output impedances, and the loop gain of feedback circuits (for stability). An ac sweep is very fast, as it requires only one sparse linear solve per frequency point.

By construction, the ac analysis cannot show any distortion, compression, or frequency conversion: the response appears only at the excitation frequency.

### S-Parameter Analysis {#sec-simulation-acsp}

The **S-parameter analysis** (`acsp` in VACASK, `.sp` in ngspice) is an ac analysis with *ports*. Each port is an excitation source with a reference impedance $Z_0$ (usually 50 Ω). With the voltage $V_i$ and the current $I_i$ flowing into port $i$, the incident and reflected power waves and the scattering parameters are [@Pozar_RF]

$$
a_i = \frac{V_i + Z_0 I_i}{2 \sqrt{Z_0}}, \quad b_i = \frac{V_i - Z_0 I_i}{2 \sqrt{Z_0}}, \quad S_{ij} = \frac{b_i}{a_j} \quad (a_k = 0 \text{ for } k \neq j).
$$ {#eq-sim-sparam}

For an amplifier, $S_{11}$ describes the input match (return loss, see @eq-return-loss), $S_{21}$ the gain, $S_{12}$ the reverse isolation, and $S_{22}$ the output match. From the same data, the stability factors $K$ and $\mu$ follow directly (@eq-rollet-stability-factor and @eq-mu-stability-factor). S-parameters are also the natural description of passive structures like inductors, transformers, couplers, and filters, which are usually characterized by electromagnetic (EM) field simulation and enter the circuit simulation as Touchstone data or as fitted lumped-element models.

### Small-Signal Noise Analysis {#sec-simulation-noise}

The **noise analysis** (`noise`) models every noise source of the circuit (thermal noise of resistors and channels, shot noise of junctions, flicker noise, see @sec-noise-types) as a stationary random source, whose power spectral density (PSD) $S_i(f)$ is evaluated at the dc operating point. For uncorrelated sources, the contributions add in power at the output:

$$
S_\mathrm{out}(f) = \sum_i \left| H_i(f) \right|^2 S_i(f),
$$ {#eq-sim-noise}

where $H_i(f)$ is the small-signal transfer function from source $i$ to the output. Correlated sources, such as the induced gate noise and the channel noise of a MOSFET (see @sec-noise-types), add cross terms, which the simulator takes into account. Simulators either solve the linearized circuit once per noise source, or obtain all $H_i(f)$ at once from a single adjoint (transposed) solve per frequency. The results are the output noise PSD, the input-referred noise (dividing by the gain), and, most valuable for design, a ranking of the **contributions** of every device and every noise mechanism. The noise factor (@eq-noise-figure) follows as the ratio of the total output noise to the part contributed by the source resistance alone. A load resistor that only models the next stage must be excluded from the output noise, as its noise is not part of the circuit under test.

The noise analysis is the standard tool for LNAs, baseband amplifiers, TIAs, and bias and reference circuits. Its key assumption, however, is a *constant* operating point. In a circuit driven by a large periodic signal, the noise sources are modulated by the signal, and noise from many frequencies is translated to the output frequency. A plain noise analysis of a mixer, a sampling circuit, or an oscillator is therefore wrong, as we will see in @sec-simulation-pnoise.

### Transient Analysis {#sec-simulation-tran}

The **transient analysis** (`tran`) makes no assumption about the waveforms. It discretizes time, $t_{n+1} = t_n + h_n$, and replaces the time derivative in @eq-sim-circuit-equations with a numerical integration formula. With the simplest one, the backward Euler method, the equations at the new time point become

$$
\mathbf{f}(\mathbf{x}_{n+1}) + \frac{\mathbf{q}(\mathbf{x}_{n+1}) - \mathbf{q}(\mathbf{x}_n)}{h_n} = \mathbf{u}(t_{n+1}),
$$ {#eq-sim-backward-euler}

which is solved for $\mathbf{x}_{n+1}$ with the Newton iteration of @eq-sim-newton. Practical simulators use the trapezoidal rule or the Gear (backward differentiation) formulas of second order, and adapt the time step $h_n$ by estimating the local truncation error.

The transient analysis is the most general one: it handles any nonlinearity, any waveform, start-up, settling, and digital control. It is therefore the reference that all other analyses can be checked against. Its drawbacks in RF circuits are:

::: {.content-hidden when-format="revealjs"}
- **Cost.** The number of time points is the simulated time divided by the step size. The step size is set by the fastest signal (the LO or RF carrier and its edges), the simulated time by the slowest effect (settling of high-Q networks and bias circuits, the IF signal, and the frequency resolution $1/T_\mathrm{sim}$ of a subsequent FFT).
- **Numerical artifacts.** The trapezoidal rule can show spurious ringing, while the Gear formulas add numerical damping, which can make an oscillator die out or attenuate a high-frequency carrier. A maximum time step that resolves the carrier is therefore mandatory. In a 160 GHz receiver testbench, for example, omitting it let the Gear integrator damp the carrier, and the IF output came out twelve times too small in a run that finished quickly and looked healthy [@Dorrer.2026].
- **Spectral analysis.** Distortion and spurs require an FFT of a waveform in steady state, with coherent sampling or windowing, resampled to a uniform time grid, and with simulator tolerances tight enough that the numerical noise floor lies well below the products of interest.
:::

::: {.content-visible when-format="revealjs"}
- **Cost**: step size set by the fastest signal, simulated time by the slowest effect
- **Numerical artifacts**: trapezoidal ringing, Gear damping, so always set a maximum time step that resolves the carrier
- **Spectral analysis**: needs steady state, coherent sampling or windowing, and tight tolerances
:::

::: {#nte-sim-tran-effort .callout-note}
## Transient Simulation Effort of a Mixer
We want to simulate the conversion gain of a downconversion mixer with $f_\mathrm{LO} = 2.4\,\text{GHz}$ and an IF around 1 MHz, with a frequency resolution of 10 kHz. The simulated time must be at least

$$
T_\mathrm{sim} \geq \frac{1}{10\,\text{kHz}} = 100\,\mu\text{s}.
$$

With 50 time points per LO period, the step size is $h = 1 / (50 \cdot 2.4\,\text{GHz}) \approx 8.3\,\text{ps}$, and we need

$$
N = \frac{T_\mathrm{sim}}{h} = 100\,\mu\text{s} \cdot 50 \cdot 2.4\,\text{GHz} = 1.2 \cdot 10^{7}
$$

time points, each requiring a Newton solve of the full circuit, and this excludes the settling time. A PSS analysis of the same mixer integrates only a few tens of LO periods ($10^3$ to $10^4$ time points, depending on the time resolution per period), and the conversion gain then follows from a PAC analysis with one linear solve per IF frequency (@sec-simulation-pac).
:::

### Comparison of the Fundamental Analyses

| Analysis | Solves | Assumption | Typical RF use |
|:-----------|:------------------|:----------------|:------------------------------|
| `op`, dc sweep | $\mathbf{f}(\mathbf{x}_0) = \mathbf{u}_\mathrm{DC}$ | static | bias point, dc transfer curves |
| `ac` | @eq-sim-ac | small signal, LTI | gain, bandwidth, impedances, loop gain |
| `acsp` | @eq-sim-ac with ports | small signal, LTI | matching, gain, isolation, stability, passives |
| `noise` | @eq-sim-noise | small signal, stationary noise | NF of LNAs and baseband, noise contributions |
| `tran` | @eq-sim-backward-euler | none | start-up, settling, switching, large-signal reference |
: Comparison of the fundamental analyses. {#tbl-sim-fundamental}

## Advanced RF Analyses {#sec-simulation-advanced}

The fundamental analyses either linearize around a constant operating point (ac, noise) or integrate the full nonlinear equations in time (tran). Many RF circuits sit in between: a **large periodic signal**, such as the LO of a mixer, the clock of a switched-capacitor (SC) filter or sampler, the carrier of a PA, or the oscillation itself in an oscillator, sets a periodically time-varying operating point, while the information-bearing signal and the noise are small. The advanced analyses exploit this structure in two steps:

1. **Large-signal step.** The periodic steady state is computed directly, either in the time domain (shooting PSS, @sec-simulation-pss) or in the frequency domain (HB, @sec-simulation-hb), without simulating the settling transient.
2. **Small-signal step.** The circuit is linearized around this periodic steady state. The resulting LPTV system is analyzed for frequency-translating transfer functions (PAC, HBAC, @sec-simulation-pac) and for cyclostationary noise (PNOISE, HBNOISE, @sec-simulation-pnoise).

Transient noise (@sec-simulation-trannoise) is the exception: it is a brute-force extension of the transient analysis, without any linearization.

### Transient Noise {#sec-simulation-trannoise}

In a **transient noise** simulation, every noise source of the circuit is replaced by a random time-domain waveform with the correct PSD within a band from $f_\mathrm{min}$ to $f_\mathrm{max}$, and injected into an ordinary transient analysis. White noise is generated from independent random samples, and flicker noise is approximated by a sum of filtered (Lorentzian) processes whose corner frequencies cover the band from $f_\mathrm{min}$ to $f_\mathrm{max}$. The samples are either held constant on a fixed time grid (zero-order hold) or integrated as stochastic differential equations along the actual time steps. To resolve the noise up to $f_\mathrm{max}$, the time step is limited to a fraction of $1/(2 f_\mathrm{max})$.

Because the circuit equations are integrated without linearization, transient noise includes in principle everything: switching, strong nonlinearity, sampling and noise folding, the conversion of noise into jitter, and even noise-induced decisions such as metastability and bit errors in comparators. In practice, it is also the numerically most fragile of all analyses, and the price is high:

::: {.content-hidden when-format="revealjs"}
- **Statistics.** Each run produces one random realization. A PSD, a jitter value, or an error probability requires long records, averaging, or many runs with different random seeds, and the frequency resolution is $1/T_\mathrm{sim}$. Estimate the uncertainty from independent seeds rather than from segments of one record. A fixed seed reproduces a run only for an unchanged netlist, so after a circuit change, a difference within the scatter of the seeds is not a result.
- **Run time.** The step size is limited by $f_\mathrm{max}$, even in parts of the waveform where the signal itself would allow large steps.
- **Band limits.** Flicker noise down to $f_\mathrm{min}$ requires $T_\mathrm{sim} \gg 1/f_\mathrm{min}$, and a default lower band edge derived from $f_\mathrm{max}$ (in VACASK, $f_\mathrm{max}/1000$) can silently remove all flicker noise at the offsets of interest. When the noise is integrated along the actual time steps, white noise extends up to the Nyquist frequency of these steps. The waveform must then be resampled at least as finely as the simulator's own steps before a PSD is computed, or out-of-band noise aliases into the band.
- **Numerical artifacts.** Device noise is tiny compared to the signals, and on stiff, strongly nonlinear circuits the random excitation itself can cause numerical errors that a noiseless run does not show. Run the analysis at two or more reduced noise amplitudes (a scaling factor such as `noisescale` in VACASK makes this easy), and use the part of the output noise power that scales with the square of the amplitude. Accept a higher-order part only if its size and order match a physical mechanism. A run at zero noise amplitude with otherwise identical settings, which uses the same time grid, shows the numerical floor.
- **Clocked circuits.** For comparators and sampled-data circuits, make sure that the run completes for the full number of decisions or cycles the statistics need, and validate the result against an independent estimate, such as an analytic $kT/C$ budget or a periodic noise analysis.
:::

::: {.content-visible when-format="revealjs"}
- **Statistics**: one realization per run, so long records, many seeds, resolution $1/T_\mathrm{sim}$
- **Run time**: step size limited by $f_\mathrm{max}$
- **Band limits**: flicker needs $T_\mathrm{sim} \gg 1/f_\mathrm{min}$, resample finely before a PSD
- **Numerical artifacts**: run at reduced noise amplitudes, keep the part that scales with the amplitude squared
- **Clocked circuits**: complete all needed decisions, validate independently
:::

Typical applications are comparators (input-referred noise from the decision statistics), sampled-data circuits and ADCs ($kT/C$ noise and the SNR including all effects), the jitter of oscillators, clock buffers, and dividers, and, increasingly important, an independent cross-check of PNOISE and HBNOISE results. Transient noise shares no solver code with the periodic analyses, but it uses the same device noise models. Their agreement therefore validates the implementation of the analyses rather than the noise models, and its statistics limit it to about a decibel.

### Periodic Steady State by Shooting (PSS) {#sec-simulation-pss}

Consider a circuit driven by large-signal sources with period $T = 1/f_0$. After the start-up transient has died out, the circuit is in its **periodic steady state** $\mathbf{x}_\mathrm{s}(t + T) = \mathbf{x}_\mathrm{s}(t)$. Let $\boldsymbol{\phi}_T(\mathbf{x}_0)$ denote the state reached after integrating the circuit equations over one period, starting from the state $\mathbf{x}_0$. The **shooting method** searches for the initial state that reproduces itself after one period [@Aprille.1972]:

$$
\boldsymbol{\phi}_T(\mathbf{x}_0) - \mathbf{x}_0 = \mathbf{0}.
$$ {#eq-sim-shooting}

This is again solved with Newton's method,

$$
\left( \mathbf{\Phi}_T - \mathbf{I} \right) \Delta \mathbf{x}_0 = \mathbf{x}_0 - \boldsymbol{\phi}_T(\mathbf{x}_0), \qquad \mathbf{\Phi}_T = \frac{\partial \boldsymbol{\phi}_T}{\partial \mathbf{x}_0},
$$ {#eq-sim-shooting-newton}

where the sensitivity matrix $\mathbf{\Phi}_T$ (the *monodromy matrix*) is computed alongside the transient integration over one period. Every Newton iteration therefore costs one period of transient simulation. For a linear circuit, the method converges in a single iteration, and a mildly nonlinear circuit needs a few. Usually, a short stabilization transient precedes the Newton loop to provide a good initial guess. In large circuits, the dense matrix $\mathbf{\Phi}_T$ would be prohibitive, and matrix-free iterative (Krylov subspace) solvers made shooting practical for circuits with thousands of nodes [@Telichevesky.1995]. VACASK currently integrates the full matrix $\mathbf{\Phi}_T$, which is fine for circuit blocks but becomes expensive for large (e.g., post-layout) netlists.

The main advantage is illustrated in @fig-sim-tran-vs-pss: a high-Q circuit that needs many periods to settle in a transient analysis (about 110 for $Q = 50$) is solved with one or a few shooting iterations of one period each, because Newton's method jumps directly to the steady state.

{{< include /content/simulation/_fig_sim_tran_vs_pss.qmd >}}

Since the integration happens in the time domain with adaptive steps, PSS handles sharp edges and strongly nonlinear behavior just as well as a transient analysis: switching mixers, SC circuits, frequency dividers, rectifiers, and switching PAs (class D, E, F). Its main limitation is that it needs a **single period**: all large-signal sources must be periodic with a common period $T$. A two-tone test with tones at 2.400 GHz and 2.401 GHz, for example, has a common period of 1 µs, i.e., 2400 carrier periods, which makes shooting inefficient. Note that only the *large* signals count: a small RF signal handled by PAC (@sec-simulation-pac) does not enter the period.

For **oscillators** (autonomous circuits), the period is unknown and becomes an additional unknown of the Newton iteration. As any time-shifted copy of a periodic solution is also a solution, a phase condition is added to make the problem well-defined. An autonomous PSS directly delivers the oscillation frequency and the steady-state waveform, without simulating the start-up. The circuit has to be kicked away from its (unstable) dc operating point by an initial condition, otherwise the analysis converges to the trivial dc solution.

::: {.callout-important}
## PSS Does Not Prove Start-Up
PSS finds a periodic solution, but it does not tell whether the circuit actually reaches it after power-up. Whether an oscillator starts reliably over all corners (or whether a divider locks into the intended mode) must still be checked with a transient analysis.
:::

From the periodic waveforms, the Fourier coefficients follow directly: harmonic distortion, the dc shift of a rectifier or power detector, the duty cycle of an LO signal, the efficiency of a PA (from the output power at the fundamental and the averaged supply power), and, for oscillators, frequency and amplitude versus a tuning voltage (i.e., the tuning curve and $K_\mathrm{VCO}$, see @sec-frequency-tuning-of-oscillators).

### Harmonic Balance (HB) {#sec-simulation-hb}

**Harmonic balance** describes every unknown by a truncated Fourier series with $K$ harmonics (not to be confused with the stability factor $K$ of @sec-amp-stability),

$$
\mathbf{x}(t) = \sum_{k=-K}^{K} \mathbf{X}_k \, e^{j k \omega_0 t}, \qquad \mathbf{X}_{-k} = \mathbf{X}_k^{*},
$$ {#eq-sim-hb-fourier}

and solves for the Fourier coefficients $\mathbf{X}_k$ directly [@Nakhla.1976]. Inserted into @eq-sim-circuit-equations, the time derivative becomes an exact multiplication by $j k \omega_0$, and the circuit equations must hold ("balance") at every harmonic:

$$
\mathbf{F}_k(\mathbf{X}) + j k \omega_0 \, \mathbf{Q}_k(\mathbf{X}) = \mathbf{U}_k, \qquad k = -K, \ldots, K.
$$ {#eq-sim-hb}

Here, $\mathbf{F}_k$ and $\mathbf{Q}_k$ are the Fourier coefficients of $\mathbf{f}(\mathbf{x}(t))$ and $\mathbf{q}(\mathbf{x}(t))$. Nonlinear device equations cannot be evaluated in the frequency domain, so HB transforms the present estimate of the spectrum into the time domain (inverse FFT), evaluates the devices at the sampled time points, and transforms the results back (FFT). All harmonics of all nodes are solved for jointly with Newton's method, so the linear system has $(2K+1)$ times as many unknowns as the circuit.

With several large tones (e.g., a two-tone test, or LO and blocker), the solution is *quasi-periodic*, and the spectrum contains all mixing products $k_1 \omega_1 + k_2 \omega_2$. HB handles this naturally, without the long simulated time that a transient analysis needs for closely spaced tones, and the spectrum is truncated, e.g., to $|k_1| + |k_2| \leq K$ ("diamond" truncation). The truncation then limits the accuracy of small intermodulation products, so check that the IM3 products rise with a slope of 3 before extrapolating an intercept point.

Strengths and weaknesses of HB are complementary to those of shooting:

::: {.content-hidden when-format="revealjs"}
- **Linear and distributed elements** are described exactly in the frequency domain, including transmission lines and, in simulators that accept them, frequency-domain data like S-parameter files from EM simulations. Such data, or a lumped model fitted to them, must be valid and passive from dc up to the highest harmonic and mixing product, not only in the band of interest.
- **High-Q circuits** pose no settling problem, as no transient is simulated.
- **Mildly nonlinear circuits** (LNAs, linear PAs, baseband amplifiers) are described accurately with a few harmonics, which makes HB very efficient for compression, IP3, and blocker simulations.
- **Strongly nonlinear circuits with sharp edges** need many harmonics, as the spectrum of a square wave decays only as $1/k$ (see @fig-sim-hb-truncation). Every additional harmonic enlarges the nonlinear system, which also becomes increasingly ill-conditioned, so accuracy has to be traded against convergence and run time, and a truncated spectrum shows Gibbs ringing. For hard-switching circuits (SC circuits, switching mixers with square-wave LO, dividers), HB may not converge at all, and PSS is the better choice.
- **Convergence** can be difficult at high drive levels. Simulators ramp the source amplitudes (source stepping), and it often helps to sweep the drive level up and use each solution as the starting point of the next one.
:::

::: {.content-visible when-format="revealjs"}
- **Linear and distributed elements**: exact, including S-parameter data
- **High-Q circuits**: no settling problem
- **Mildly nonlinear circuits**: few harmonics, very efficient ($P_\mathrm{1dB}$, IP3, blockers)
- **Sharp edges**: many harmonics, ill-conditioning, Gibbs ringing (@fig-sim-hb-truncation), may not converge, so use PSS
- **Convergence**: ramp the drive level (source stepping, sweeps)
:::

{{< include /content/simulation/_fig_sim_hb_truncation.qmd >}}

The harmonic count $K$ is the key accuracy parameter of HB, just as the step size is for a transient analysis. Too small a $K$ does not show up as a convergence failure: Newton's method converges, but to the solution of the truncated problem. The convergence in $K$ need not be monotonic either, so two neighboring values that agree prove little. Compare with a much larger $K$ or, better, with an independent engine (PSS), and repeat the check over the whole drive sweep, as the required $K$ grows with the drive level: a value that is sufficient at the nominal level can be several dB off beyond the 1 dB compression point. Oscillators can also be simulated with HB, using an autonomous variant that adds the unknown frequency and a phase condition, similar to the autonomous PSS. Check whether your simulator supports it (in VACASK, oscillators are solved with the autonomous `pss`).

| Property | PSS (shooting) | HB |
|:-------------------------|:---------------------|:---------------------|
| Domain | time | frequency (devices evaluated in time) |
| Unknowns | initial state $\mathbf{x}_0$ | Fourier coefficients $\mathbf{X}_k$ |
| Sharp edges, switching | well suited | many harmonics, may not converge |
| Mildly nonlinear | well suited | very efficient |
| Distributed elements, S-parameter data | need a time-domain model | exact (simulator-dependent) |
| Several incommensurate large tones | not possible | well suited |
| High-Q, long settling | efficient | efficient |
| Oscillators | autonomous PSS | autonomous HB (simulator-dependent) |
| Small-signal and noise analyses | PAC, PNOISE | HBAC, HBNOISE |
: Comparison of shooting (PSS) and harmonic balance (HB). {#tbl-sim-pss-hb}

### Periodic Small-Signal Analysis (PAC, HBAC) {#sec-simulation-pac}

We now apply a small signal $\Delta \mathbf{u}(t)$ to a circuit in its periodic steady state $\mathbf{x}_\mathrm{s}(t)$ and linearize @eq-sim-circuit-equations around $\mathbf{x}_\mathrm{s}(t)$:

$$
\mathbf{G}(t) \, \Delta \mathbf{x}(t) + \frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t} \left[ \mathbf{C}(t) \, \Delta \mathbf{x}(t) \right] = \Delta \mathbf{u}(t).
$$ {#eq-sim-lptv}

In contrast to @eq-sim-ac, the Jacobians $\mathbf{G}(t) = \partial \mathbf{f} / \partial \mathbf{x}$ and $\mathbf{C}(t) = \partial \mathbf{q} / \partial \mathbf{x}$ are now evaluated along $\mathbf{x}_\mathrm{s}(t)$ and are periodic in time. The small-signal circuit is a **linear periodically time-varying (LPTV)** system. Exactly like the time-variant mixer of @sec-mixer-time-variant, such a system converts an input at the offset frequency $f$ into outputs at all **sidebands** $f + k f_0$. We therefore expand the Jacobians into Fourier series, $\mathbf{G}(t) = \sum_p \mathbf{G}_p e^{j p \omega_0 t}$ (same for $\mathbf{C}$), and the excitation and the response into sideband phasors, $\Delta \mathbf{u}(t) = \sum_k \Delta \mathbf{U}_k e^{j (\omega + k \omega_0) t}$ and $\Delta \mathbf{x}(t) = \sum_k \Delta \mathbf{X}_k e^{j (\omega + k \omega_0) t}$. Collecting the terms at each sideband yields the **conversion matrix** equation [@Kundert.1999]

$$
\sum_{l=-K}^{K} \left[ \mathbf{G}_{k-l} + j (\omega + k \omega_0) \, \mathbf{C}_{k-l} \right] \Delta \mathbf{X}_l = \Delta \mathbf{U}_k, \qquad k = -K, \ldots, K,
$$ {#eq-sim-conversion-matrix}

which couples the sidebands $l$ to the sidebands $k$ through the harmonics $\mathbf{G}_{k-l}$ and $\mathbf{C}_{k-l}$ of the time-varying operating point. Without time variation, only $\mathbf{G}_0$ and $\mathbf{C}_0$ are nonzero, and @eq-sim-conversion-matrix falls apart into independent copies of the ac analysis of @eq-sim-ac. Solving @eq-sim-conversion-matrix for a source at sideband $l$ and observing sideband $k$ gives the **harmonic transfer function** $H_{k,l}(f)$. The offset frequency $f$ is swept, and each point requires one linear solve of a system with $(2K+1)$ times as many unknowns as the circuit. This is far cheaper than a transient simulation, but the cost grows quickly with $K$, as discussed below.

{{< include /content/simulation/_fig_sim_pac_sidebands.qmd >}}

@fig-sim-pac-sidebands shows the frequency grid for a downconversion mixer. The LO is the large signal, the RF and IF are small signals:

::: {.content-hidden when-format="revealjs"}
- The **conversion gain** is the transfer from the RF at $f_\mathrm{LO} + f$ (input sideband $+1$) to the IF at $f$ (output sideband $0$), i.e., $H_{0,+1}(f)$, swept over the IF band in a single analysis.
- The **image response** is $H_{0,-1}(f)$ from $f_\mathrm{LO} - f$. A single mixer converts both sidebands with equal magnitude. In an I/Q (image-reject) receiver, the ratio of the two, evaluated after the I and Q paths are combined, gives the image rejection.
- The **harmonic responses** $H_{0,\pm 3}(f)$ show how much of an interferer around $3 f_\mathrm{LO}$ appears at the IF, which matters for switching mixers in wideband receivers (compare the Fourier series of the switching function in @sec-mixer-time-variant).
- For an **upconversion mixer**, the input is at the baseband sideband $0$ and the output at sideband $\pm 1$.
:::

::: {.content-visible when-format="revealjs"}
- **Conversion gain**: $H_{0,+1}(f)$, RF at $f_\mathrm{LO} + f$ to IF at $f$
- **Image response**: $H_{0,-1}(f)$
- **Harmonic responses**: $H_{0,\pm 3}(f)$, interferers around $3 f_\mathrm{LO}$
- **Upconversion**: input at sideband $0$, output at $\pm 1$
:::

::: {.callout-important}
## Why an AC Analysis of a Mixer Fails
An ac analysis linearizes around the dc operating point, where the LO source sits at its dc value. The mixer is "frozen" in one LO state, the circuit is LTI, and no frequency conversion takes place: the ac analysis shows at most a feedthrough at the RF frequency, but no IF output. Frequency-converting circuits need PAC or HBAC.
:::

Further applications of the periodic small-signal analyses are:

::: {.content-hidden when-format="revealjs"}
- **SC filters and sampling circuits**, where the clock is the large signal. The transfer from input sideband $k$ to output sideband $0$ quantifies aliasing, i.e., how much of an input at $f + k f_\mathrm{clk}$ appears at $f$.
- **N-path filters and passive mixers**, where the input impedance around $f_\mathrm{LO}$ (see @eq-npath-impedance) is obtained from the transfer at the same sideband.
- **Power detectors**, whose video response (the detected baseband output for an amplitude-modulated input) is the transfer from sideband $\pm 1$ around the carrier to sideband $0$.
- **Amplifiers under a large blocker**, where the blocker is the large signal and the wanted signal the small one. This directly shows the gain reduction by desensitization (see @eq-linearity-double-a).
- **Chopper amplifiers**, where the chopping clock is the large signal. The transfer from input sideband $0$ to output sideband $0$ is the gain after demodulation, while the transfers to the sidebands around the chopping harmonics show how much of the signal appears as ripple.
:::

::: {.content-visible when-format="revealjs"}
- **SC filters, sampling circuits**: transfer including aliasing
- **N-path filters, passive mixers**: input impedance around $f_\mathrm{LO}$ (@eq-npath-impedance)
- **Power detectors**: video response
- **Amplifiers under a blocker**: desensitization (@eq-linearity-double-a)
- **Chopper amplifiers**: gain after demodulation, ripple at the chopping harmonics
:::

**PAC** and **HBAC** solve the same @eq-sim-conversion-matrix. They differ only in the large-signal solution underneath: PAC builds on the shooting PSS (single fundamental, any waveform shape), HBAC on harmonic balance (also quasi-periodic, e.g., with an LO and a large blocker as two tones, but limited by the harmonic count of the HB solution). The naming follows the engine: the analyses on top of shooting carry a "P" (PAC, PNOISE, and in some simulators PXF and PSP for transfer functions and S-parameters), those on top of harmonic balance carry "HB" (HBAC, HBNOISE, HBXF, HBSP).

The truncation $K$ of @eq-sim-conversion-matrix must cover the harmonic content of $\mathbf{G}(t)$ and $\mathbf{C}(t)$: a few harmonics are enough for smooth waveforms, while hard-switching circuits like SC filters with steep clock edges can require tens to hundreds of harmonics. For the large signal, the PSS-based analyses have a clear advantage: the periodic steady state is computed in the time domain and is not truncated at all, while HB has to carry all these harmonics in its nonlinear system. In the [Gilbert-cell example of VACASK](https://codeberg.org/arpadbuermen/VACASK/src/branch/main/demo/gilbert/gilbert.sim), for instance, a large trapezoidal LO drives the switching quad: HB, and with it HBAC, currently does not converge, while PAC delivers the sidebands with 20 harmonics.

The small-signal step, however, is truncated in both families when it is solved with @eq-sim-conversion-matrix, as in VACASK. Every nonzero Jacobian entry becomes a dense $(2K+1) \times (2K+1)$ block, so the memory grows with $K^2$. With hard switching, the truncation itself becomes the limit: the truncated Fourier series of a switch conductance does not vanish while the switch is off, so the switch leaks in the small-signal model. On high-impedance nodes, such as the virtual ground of an SC integrator, this spurious leak can falsify the low-frequency gain and noise until $K$ reaches several hundred, which may be impractical. Check the convergence in $K$ (keeping in mind that it need not be monotonic, see @sec-simulation-hb), and fall back to transient simulations where it is not reached.

### Periodic Noise Analysis (PNOISE, HBNOISE) {#sec-simulation-pnoise}

The noise analysis of @eq-sim-noise misses two effects that a large periodic signal introduces:

1. **Modulation.** The noise sources depend on the time-varying operating point: channel thermal noise follows the channel conductance (see @sec-noise-types), shot noise follows the current $I(t)$, and flicker noise depends on the bias as well. Such a source can be written as $n_i(t) = m_i(t) \, w_i(t)$, with a stationary noise process $w_i(t)$ and a periodic modulation $m_i(t)$. Its statistics vary periodically with time, so the noise is **cyclostationary**.
2. **Frequency translation.** The LPTV transfer of @eq-sim-conversion-matrix moves noise from all sidebands $f + l f_0$ to the output frequency $f$, which is called **noise folding**.

Combining both effects, with $M_{i,m}$ the Fourier coefficients of $m_i(t)$, $S_i$ the PSD of the stationary process $w_i(t)$, and $H_{i,k}(f)$ the transfer function from source $i$ at sideband $k$ to the output, gives the output PSD [@Okumura.1993; @Roychowdhury.1998]

$$
S_\mathrm{out}(f) = \sum_i \sum_{l} \left| \sum_{k} H_{i,k}(f) \, M_{i,k-l} \right|^2 S_i(f + l f_0),
$$ {#eq-sim-pnoise}

with all spectral densities written two-sided. For a constant operating point ($M_{i,0} = 1$, all other coefficients zero, and $H_{i,k} = 0$ for $k \neq 0$), @eq-sim-pnoise reduces to @eq-sim-noise. A single adjoint solve per offset frequency delivers the transfer functions of all sources, and the results are again broken down into contributions per device and per noise mechanism. **PNOISE** builds on the shooting PSS, **HBNOISE** on harmonic balance, exactly as PAC and HBAC. HBNOISE can also start from a multi-tone (quasi-periodic) HB solution, e.g., to obtain the noise figure of a mixer with an LO and a large blocker applied at the same time.

::: {#nte-sim-noise-folding .callout-note}
## Noise Folding in an Ideal Switching Mixer
An ideal double-balanced switching mixer multiplies the RF input by a square wave toggling between $+1$ and $-1$ with 50 % duty cycle (see @sec-mixer-time-variant), whose Fourier coefficients have the magnitude $|c_k| = 2/(\pi |k|)$ for odd $k$ and vanish for even $k$. The switches are noiseless, and the only noise is the white thermal noise of the source resistance, with the PSD $S_\mathrm{n}$ at every frequency. The noise from each sideband $k$ folds to the IF with the weight $|c_k|^2$. By Parseval's theorem, the sum of all weights equals the time average of the squared switching function, which is one:

$$
S_\mathrm{out} = S_\mathrm{n} \sum_{k} |c_k|^2 = S_\mathrm{n}.
$$

The wanted RF signal at sideband $+1$ is converted with the power gain $|c_1|^2 = 4/\pi^2$. In the single-sideband (SSB) noise factor, only the source noise at the signal frequency counts as input noise, hence

$$
F_\mathrm{SSB} = \frac{S_\mathrm{out}}{|c_1|^2 S_\mathrm{n}} = \frac{\pi^2}{4} \approx 3.9\,\text{dB}.
$$

If the signal occupies both sidebands $\pm 1$ (as in a direct-conversion receiver), the source noise of both counts as input noise, and the double-sideband (DSB) noise factor is $F_\mathrm{DSB} = \pi^2/8 \approx 0.9\,\text{dB}$, i.e., 3 dB lower. An analysis that keeps only the sidebands $\pm 1$ ($K = 1$) would miss the 19 % of the noise folded from around $3 f_\mathrm{LO}$, $5 f_\mathrm{LO}$, and so on, and underestimate the noise figure by 0.9 dB (@fig-sim-noise-folding).
:::

{{< include /content/simulation/_fig_sim_noise_folding.qmd >}}

The periodic noise analyses are required wherever a large periodic signal modulates the noise or translates it in frequency:

::: {.content-hidden when-format="revealjs"}
- **Mixers**: SSB and DSB noise figure, including the noise folded from the image and from the sidebands of the LO harmonics, and the flicker noise of the switches that the LO translates to the IF (compare the discussion of passive and active mixers in @sec-mixer-time-variant).
- **Sampling and SC circuits**: wideband switch noise folds into the baseband ($kT/C$ noise). Many harmonics are needed, and with steep clock edges the conversion matrix may not converge in practice (see @sec-simulation-pac), so transient noise or an analytic $kT/C$ budget are the alternatives.
- **Power detectors**: the noise with the LO (or the input carrier) applied, which can differ substantially from the quiescent noise analysis.
- **Amplifiers under a blocker**: the noise figure in the presence of a large interferer.
- **Chopper amplifiers**: the flicker noise that remains at baseband after chopping, and the white noise folded back from the chopping harmonics.
- **Oscillators**: the phase noise. An oscillator's noise is cyclostationary by nature, and its noise sources are converted into phase noise in a time-dependent way, which the impulse sensitivity function describes [@Hajimiri.1998]. A rigorous nonlinear analysis shows that the phase of an oscillator diffuses like a random walk, so that the output spectrum is a Lorentzian that stays finite at the carrier, whereas a linear analysis predicts phase noise that grows without bound towards the carrier [@Demir.2000]. Commercial RF simulators compute the phase noise with a periodic noise analysis around an *autonomous* steady state, including the upconverted flicker noise of the $1/f^3$ region, which Leeson's equation (@eq-leeson-equation) does not cover. In any simulator, such an analysis holds only down to the offset frequency where the harmonic truncation starts to pin the phase: a phase noise that flattens towards the carrier instead of rising with $1/f^2$ is a symptom, not a result. VACASK's `pnoise` also accepts an autonomous PSS (`oscillator=1`), but its documentation does not cover phase noise yet, and the example that ships with the simulator extracts the phase noise from a transient noise simulation. For oscillators with logic-like edges, such as ring oscillators, transient noise is usually the method of choice anyway. A plain noise analysis of an oscillator is meaningless, as it linearizes around the unstable dc operating point.
:::

::: {.content-visible when-format="revealjs"}
- **Mixers**: SSB/DSB NF incl. image and harmonic folding, LO-translated flicker noise
- **Sampling, SC circuits**: $kT/C$ noise from folded wideband noise
- **Power detectors**: noise with the LO or carrier applied
- **Amplifiers under a blocker**: blocker noise figure
- **Chopper amplifiers**: residual flicker noise, white noise folded from the chopping harmonics
- **Oscillators**: phase noise incl. $1/f^3$ region from periodic noise (valid down to where truncation pins the phase) or transient noise, but never from a plain noise analysis
:::

For the sweep of the offset frequency, keep in mind that the upconverted flicker noise forms narrow skirts around every harmonic of the large signal. A coarse logarithmic sweep easily steps over them, and a point exactly at a harmonic is undefined for $1/f$ noise. A dense grid near (but not at) the harmonics resolves them.

## Choosing the Right Analysis {#sec-simulation-selection}

@tbl-sim-advanced summarizes the advanced analyses, and @fig-sim-decision condenses the selection into two questions: is there a large periodic signal that sets the operating point, and how sharp are the resulting waveforms?

| Analysis | Builds on | Linearized | Captures | Main limitation |
|:-----------|:----------|:------------|:---------------------|:------------------|
| transient noise | tran | no | in principle everything: switching, folding, jitter, decisions | statistics, run time, numerical artifacts |
| PSS | shooting (time) | no | periodic steady state, harmonics, oscillation frequency | one common period |
| HB | Fourier series | no | (quasi-)periodic steady state, IM products | many harmonics for sharp edges |
| PAC, HBAC | PSS, HB | yes (LPTV) | conversion gain, sideband transfer, aliasing | small signals only |
| PNOISE, HBNOISE | PSS, HB | yes (LPTV) | cyclostationary noise, folding, mixer NF | small noise only |
: Comparison of the advanced RF analyses. {#tbl-sim-advanced}

{{< include /content/simulation/_fig_sim_decision.qmd >}}

For typical RF building blocks, @tbl-sim-applications lists the key metrics and the recommended analyses. The first analysis in each row is usually the workhorse, and the others refine or cross-check it.

| Circuit | Key metrics | Recommended analyses |
|:------------------|:--------------------|:----------------------------------|
| LNA | match, gain, NF, stability, $P_\mathrm{1dB}$, IIP3, blocker NF | op, acsp and noise, HB for $P_\mathrm{1dB}$ and two-tone IIP3, HBAC and HBNOISE with a blocker |
| Mixer | conversion gain, SSB/DSB NF, IIP3, image and harmonic rejection | PSS (hard-switching LO) or HB, PAC or HBAC, PNOISE or HBNOISE, two-tone HB for IIP3 |
| Oscillator, VCO | start-up, frequency, tuning range, phase noise | tran for start-up, autonomous PSS, transient noise or periodic noise around the autonomous PSS (simulator-dependent) |
| SC circuits, sampling, N-path | transfer incl. aliasing, settling, $kT/C$ noise | tran, PSS, PAC and PNOISE if they converge in $K$ (not HB), transient noise |
| Power detector | responsivity, compression, video bandwidth, NEP, NF | HB or PSS power sweep, HBAC or PAC, noise with the LO off, HBNOISE or PNOISE with the LO on, transient noise |
| Power amplifier | output power, efficiency, AM/AM, AM/PM, harmonics | HB power sweep (with EM models of the matching network), PSS for switching PAs, tran |
| Divider, LO generation | operating range, duty cycle, I/Q phase error, jitter | tran, PSS, PNOISE or transient noise for jitter |
| Chopper amplifier | gain, ripple, residual flicker noise | tran, PSS with PAC and PNOISE |
| Comparator, latch | offset, noise, metastability | tran, transient noise |
| Passives | Q, S-parameters | acsp with EM-derived models |
: Recommended analyses for typical RF building blocks. {#tbl-sim-applications}

A complete PLL contains time constants from the VCO period (ns) to the loop settling time (µs), which makes a full transistor-level steady-state simulation very expensive. In practice, the blocks (VCO, divider, phase detector, charge pump) are characterized individually with the analyses above, and the loop is evaluated with the linear phase-domain model of @sec-pll and with behavioral transient simulations.

Whatever analysis is used, a result is only trustworthy after it has been checked:

::: {.content-hidden when-format="revealjs"}
- **Convergence parameters.** Increase the harmonic count (HB, PAC, PNOISE) well beyond the value that seems sufficient, tighten the maximum time step and the tolerances (tran), and lengthen the stabilization time (PSS) until the result no longer changes, and repeat these checks at the highest drive level.
- **Independent methods.** HB and PSS compute the same steady state with different algorithms, and where both converge, PAC must agree with HBAC and PNOISE with HBNOISE. PAC or HBAC conversion gain can be compared with a two-tone transient, and PNOISE or HBNOISE with transient noise at reduced noise amplitude. With the large signal switched off, PNOISE and HBNOISE must reproduce the plain noise analysis.
- **Simulator messages.** A simulation that finishes is not necessarily a correct one. Check the log for aborted analyses, convergence warnings, and devices that were silently dropped from the netlist. Neither a zero exit status nor an existing result file proves that an analysis ran, so delete old results before rerunning.
:::

::: {.content-visible when-format="revealjs"}
- **Convergence parameters**: harmonics, time step, tolerances, stabilization time, also at the highest drive
- **Independent methods**: HB vs. PSS, PAC vs. HBAC, PNOISE vs. HBNOISE, PAC vs. two-tone tran, PNOISE vs. transient noise, PNOISE without large signal vs. noise
- **Simulator messages**: a finished run is not a correct one
:::

::: {#nte-sim-power-detector .callout-note}
## Example: A 160 GHz Power Detector
The open-source SPARX receiver [@Dorrer.2026] contains a Schottky-diode power detector at 160 GHz, characterized with VACASK as a mixer with a 159 GHz LO. Its testbenches use most of the analyses of this appendix:

- **HB** power sweep for the transfer curve (responsivity and compression), cross-checked with **PSS** at nine drive levels. The two agree within 1.2 % over an input range of 80 dB.
- **HBAC** for the conversion gain of each sideband to the IF and the video bandwidth, cross-checked with **PAC** (within 0.03 dB).
- **noise** (LO off) and **HBNOISE** (LO on) for the noise figure: the LO raises the output noise, so the noise analysis at the dc operating point is 1.2 dB to 2.6 dB optimistic over the IF band, and far more at high LO drive. **PNOISE** reproduces HBNOISE within 0.2 dB.
- **Transient noise** with the LO on, run at reduced noise amplitudes and reduced to its linear part, agrees with HBNOISE within about 1 dB.
:::

## Simulator Support {#sec-simulation-tools}

@tbl-sim-tools lists the analyses of this appendix in the two open-source simulators used in this course, in the ngspice release 47 and the VACASK version of the IIC-OSIC-TOOLS container 2026.10. The ngspice development branch already contains a driven PSS with PAC, PNOISE, PXF and PSP, and quasi-periodic analyses (`qpss`, `qpac`, `qpnoise`), which are not part of a release yet (November 2026). Among the commercial RF simulators, Cadence Spectre RF offers all of them, plus further variants like quasi-periodic shooting and periodic transfer functions and S-parameters (PXF, PSP), while Keysight ADS is built around harmonic balance with its small-signal and noise variants, and adds envelope simulation for modulated signals.

| Analysis | VACASK (container 2026.10) | ngspice 47 |
|:-----------------------|:------------------------|:------------------------|
| dc operating point, dc sweep | `op`, `op` inside a `sweep` | `.op`, `.dc` |
| ac | `ac` | `.ac` |
| S-parameters | `acsp` | `.sp` |
| noise | `noise` | `.noise` |
| transient | `tran` | `.tran` |
| transient noise | `tran` with `noisefmax` (device noise) | `.tran` with `trnoise` sources |
| PSS | `pss` (driven and autonomous) | `.pss` (experimental, autonomous only) |
| HB | `hb` (single and multi-tone) | not available |
| PAC, PNOISE | `pac`, `pnoise` | not available |
| HBAC, HBNOISE | `hbac`, `hbnoise` | not available |
: Analyses in the open-source simulators VACASK and ngspice. {#tbl-sim-tools}

The following VACASK excerpt shows the two-step flow of @sec-simulation-advanced for a downconversion mixer: the periodic steady state with the LO is computed and stored once, and the conversion gain and the noise figure are evaluated around it. The RF source carries a unit small-signal excitation at sideband $+1$, and the IF output (node `out`) is observed at sideband $0$. Device models and the mixer itself are omitted, and the syntax is that of the VACASK version above (older builds treated `pss` as autonomous by default and used other parameter names). The noisy source resistance supplies the input noise. In the pumped circuit, its contribution at the output also contains its noise folded from the image and the harmonic sidebands. The SSB noise factor therefore divides the output noise by the source noise converted from the signal sideband alone, which is $4 k T R_\mathrm{s}$ times the power gain `gain` that `pnoise` reports for the input sideband (as in @nte-sim-noise-folding), and not by the total contribution of the source resistance.

```text
// LO: large-signal sine, RF: small-signal tone at sideband +1 (f_LO + f)
vlo (lo 0) vsource type="sine" sinedc=0 ampl=0.5 freq=2.4G
vrf (rfs 0) vsource dc=0 spur={1} smag=[1]
rs (rfs rf) resistor r=50

control
  var flo=2.4G
  analysis op1 op
  // large signal: periodic steady state with the LO, stored for reuse
  analysis pss1 pss tper=1/flo tstab=20/flo store="lo_ss"
  // conversion gain from the RF (sideband +1) to the IF (sideband 0)
  analysis pac1 pac ( ic="lo_ss" psssolve=0 truncharm=40 outharm=0
                      from=100k to=100M mode="dec" points=10 )
  // output noise at the IF, gain from the RF at sideband +1 (SSB NF)
  analysis pn1 pnoise ( ic="lo_ss" psssolve=0 truncharm=40
                        in="vrf" inharm=1 out="out" outharm=0
                        from=100k to=100M mode="dec" points=10 )
endc
```

The harmonic-balance flow with `hb`, `hbac`, and `hbnoise` is analogous, with three differences: the large signal is described by its fundamental frequencies and harmonic count (e.g., `freq=[2.4G] nharm=9`) instead of the period, a stored solution is reused with `nodeset="lo_ss" hbsolve=0`, and spurs are given as tone-weight vectors (e.g., `spur={[1]}`, `outspur=[0]`, `inspur=[1]`). VACASK ships worked examples for a [Gilbert-cell mixer](https://codeberg.org/arpadbuermen/VACASK/src/branch/main/demo/gilbert/gilbert.sim) in multiplier mode (where PAC is compared with HBAC and PNOISE with HBNOISE) and in switching mode (where VACASK's HB currently does not converge, but PAC and PNOISE do), for the PAC analysis of an [SC filter](https://codeberg.org/arpadbuermen/VACASK/src/branch/main/demo/sc/lpfilter.sim), and for the phase noise of an [oscillator from transient noise](https://codeberg.org/arpadbuermen/VACASK/src/branch/main/demo/trannoise/osc.sim). Further examples at circuit level, including the 160 GHz power detector, are found in the [testbenches of the SPARX repository](https://github.com/iic-jku/SG13CMOS_SPARX/tree/main/testbenches/xschem) [@Dorrer.2026].

## Summary {#sec-simulation-summary}

::: {.callout-important}
## Key Takeaways
- **op, ac, acsp, noise** linearize around a constant operating point: fast and insightful, but blind to distortion, frequency conversion, and noise folding.
- **tran** is the general reference, but RF time scales make it expensive, and a maximum time step is mandatory.
- **PSS** (time domain) and **HB** (frequency domain) find the periodic steady state directly. PSS suits switching circuits and oscillators, HB mildly nonlinear and multi-tone problems and circuits with distributed elements.
- **PAC, HBAC** and **PNOISE, HBNOISE** linearize around this steady state (LPTV) and give conversion gain, aliasing, and cyclostationary noise including folding.
- **Transient noise** captures everything in principle, at a high cost and with numerical pitfalls. Run at reduced noise amplitude, it is an independent cross-check.
- Increase harmonics, tighten time steps, and compare independent methods before trusting a result.
:::
